modules.title: Data Contracts
modules.summary: A data contract is an explicit agreement between data producers and consumers: schema, semantics, freshness, and ownership — written down and enforced. This module teaches contracts as the analyst's defense against silent upstream breakage: how to read them, what to demand in them, and how they connect to dbt tests and SLAs.
objectives: Define a data contract and its core elements: schema, semantics, freshness/SLA, ownership, change policy
Distinguish schema contracts from semantic contracts and explain why both matter
Read a contract and translate it into concrete dbt tests and monitoring checks
Negotiate contract terms with a producer team: what to ask for and what to concede
Describe how contracts prevent the 'silent breakage' class of pipeline failures

notes.title: What a data contract is (and isn't)
notes.body:
- A data contract is a documented, versioned agreement: 'the orders feed will contain these columns with these types and meanings, refreshed by 6 AM daily, owned by the checkout team, with 7 days notice before breaking changes.'
- It is NOT just a schema file. Schema says 'column amount is NUMERIC'; the contract adds semantics ('amount is in USD, refunds excluded'), freshness ('by 6 AM ET'), and ownership ('checkout-team@').
- Without a contract, every upstream change is a surprise: a renamed column breaks your mart at 7 AM and you find out from the stakeholder, not the producer.
- With a contract, breaking changes are announced, versioned, and migration-planned — the failure mode shifts from 'silent breakage' to 'scheduled migration'.

```yaml
# contract: orders feed v3 (example structure, adapt to your org's format)
contract: orders-feed
version: 3
owner: checkout-team@
schema:
  - {name: order_id, type: string, required: true}
  - {name: amount, type: numeric, required: true,
     semantics: 'USD, refunds excluded; see refunds table'}
  - {name: order_date, type: date, required: true}
freshness: {sla: '06:00 ET daily', late_policy: 'page owner after 30 min'}
change_policy: {breaking_notice_days: 7, channel: '#data-contracts'}
```

notes.title: Schema vs semantics: the two halves
notes.body:
- Schema contract: names, types, nullability, allowed values. Machine-checkable — this is what becomes dbt tests and pipeline assertions.
- Semantic contract: what the fields MEAN. 'amount' excluding refunds vs including them is a semantic difference no type checker catches — and it's the difference between a right and wrong revenue number.
- The analyst's job: when a number looks off, check semantics first ('did the definition of active_user change?'), schema second.
- Document semantics where the data is consumed (dbt column descriptions, semantic layer definitions) — a contract nobody can find is decoration.

```yaml
# The same schema, two different semantics -> two different revenues
columns:
  - name: amount
    tests: [not_null]
    description: >-
      SEMANTICS (contract v3): USD gross merchandise value at order time,
      refunds EXCLUDED (see refunds table), tax included. Changed 2026-09-01:
      previously included refunds. Historical comparison must note the break.
```

```sql
-- A semantic change the schema can't catch: definition of 'active'
-- Contract v2: active = logged in within 30d. Contract v3: within 7d.
-- Your dashboard drops 40% overnight with zero schema change.
-- Fix: version the metric definition, annotate the break, never silently splice.
```

notes.title: From contract to enforcement: tests and monitors
notes.body:
- Every contract clause becomes something executable: schema -> dbt generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values); freshness SLA -> a recency monitor ('max(order_date) older than 26h -> alert'); change policy -> CI check that diffs the contract file.
- Consumer-side: your staging models assert the contract on ingest — fail fast at the boundary instead of propagating bad data into marts.
- Versioning: contracts are versioned (v3), and consumers pin to a version. The producer supports v2 and v3 during the migration window, then retires v2 per the notice policy.
- Escalation path in the contract: who gets paged, in what channel, with what severity — agreed BEFORE the 6 AM failure, not during it.

```sql
-- tests/freshness_orders.sql: contract SLA as a singular test (0 rows = fresh)
SELECT MAX(order_date) AS latest
FROM {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
HAVING MAX(order_date) < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
-- Violation rows -> the 06:00 ET SLA from the contract is breached.
```

notes.title: Negotiating a contract: what analysts should demand
notes.body:
- Ask for: explicit nullability per column, allowed-value sets for codes/statuses, the freshness SLA in writing, a named owner (team + channel), and the breaking-change notice period.
- Concede gracefully: you can't demand real-time from a batch source; negotiate the SLA you actually need ('6 AM is fine; what I need is the page when it's late').
- Bring evidence: 'last quarter, three silent schema changes cost us two dashboard incidents' beats 'contracts are best practice'.
- Review cadence: contracts rot. Reconfirm semantics quarterly for your top-5 critical feeds — definitions drift even when schemas don't.

```text
Analyst's contract request (template):
1. Schema: column names/types/nullability + allowed values for codes.
2. Semantics: one-line definition per business-critical field.
3. Freshness: SLA timestamp + late-notification channel.
4. Ownership: team + on-call channel.
5. Change policy: notice period for breaking vs additive changes.
6. Versioning: contract version pinned by consumers; migration window.
Send this to the producer team; track the response like any dependency.
```

cards.back: A documented, versioned agreement on schema, semantics, freshness, ownership, and change policy between data producers and consumers.
Schema: names/types/nullability (machine-checkable). Semantics: what fields MEAN (refunds excluded? active = 7d or 30d?) — no type checker catches this.
Upstream changes with no notice that break downstream silently — the failure class contracts convert into scheduled migrations.
Schema -> dbt tests; freshness SLA -> recency monitor; change policy -> CI diff on the contract file.
Assert the contract in staging models on ingest — bad data fails there, never propagates into marts.
Contracts are versioned; consumers pin a version; producers support old+new during the migration window, then retire per notice policy.
Nullability, allowed values, freshness SLA in writing, named owner + channel, breaking-change notice period.
Definitions drift even when schemas don't — reconfirm semantics quarterly for top critical feeds.

quiz.q: Your revenue dashboard breaks at 7 AM after the checkout team renames amount to total_amount with no notice. The contract concept that prevents recurrence:
choices: A data contract with schema + 7-day breaking-change notice + named owner, so renames are announced and migration-planned
quiz.explain: Contracts convert silent breakage into scheduled, announced migrations. (Module 48)

quiz.q: amount is NUMERIC and not null, but revenue is wrong because refunds are now included. Which contract half failed?
choices: The semantic contract — the MEANING of amount changed with no schema change
quiz.explain: Semantics (what fields mean) is invisible to type checks — the classic silent break. (Module 48)

quiz.q: The contract promises freshness by 06:00 ET daily. How do you enforce it?
choices: A recency check (e.g. singular test: max(order_date) older than 1 day -> violation rows -> alert)
Email the owner daily asking if it's fresh
quiz.explain: SLA clauses become executable monitors; violations become alerts. (Module 48)

quiz.q: Producer announces contract v4 with a renamed column, supporting v3 for 30 days. You should:
choices: Pin v3, plan the migration to v4 inside the window, test, then cut over — per the change policy
quiz.explain: Versioned contracts + migration windows are the designed path — use them. (Module 48)

quiz.q: Where should field semantics ('amount excludes refunds') be documented so analysts actually find it?
choices: In a chat thread from March
Where data is consumed: dbt column descriptions / semantic layer definitions — a contract nobody can find is decoration
quiz.explain: Semantics must live at the point of consumption, not in an unread wiki. (Module 48)

quiz.q: Your 'active users' metric drops 40% overnight with zero schema change. First hypothesis:
choices: A semantic change upstream (e.g. active redefined from 30d to 7d) — check semantics before schema
quiz.explain: Definition drift with stable schema is the signature of a semantic break. (Module 48)

quiz.q: In negotiation, the producer says real-time is impossible; the feed is batch. Your move:
choices: Concede real-time; negotiate what you actually need: a written 6 AM SLA plus a page when it's late
quiz.explain: Negotiate the SLA you need and the escalation path — not an impossible architecture. (Module 48)

quiz.q: Why do staging models assert the contract on ingest instead of checking in marts?
choices: Fail fast at the boundary: bad data stops at staging instead of propagating into every downstream mart
quiz.explain: Boundary assertions contain the blast radius to one layer. (Module 48)

modules.title: Semantic Layers
modules.summary: A semantic layer defines business metrics once — 'revenue', 'active user', 'churn' — so every dashboard, notebook, and AI query computes them identically. This module teaches metric definition, dimensions vs measures, the single-source-of-truth payoff, and the governance discipline that keeps metric sprawl from returning.
objectives: Define a semantic layer and explain the metric-sprawl problem it solves
Distinguish dimensions, measures, and metric definitions with correct grain
Write a metric definition (YAML-style) with aggregation, filters, and time grain
Explain how a semantic layer serves BI tools, notebooks, and AI assistants consistently
Apply governance: naming, ownership, certification, and deprecation of metrics

notes.title: The metric-sprawl problem
notes.body:
- Without a semantic layer: Sales defines revenue as 'bookings including tax', Finance as 'recognized excluding refunds', and the exec dashboard shows a third number — three 'revenues', zero trust.
- Root cause: metric logic lives inside individual dashboards and notebooks, copied and subtly mutated each time.
- A semantic layer centralizes definitions: each metric is defined ONCE (name, logic, grain, owner) and every consumer — dashboard, notebook, AI assistant — queries the definition, not a copy.
- The payoff is trust: 'revenue' means the same everywhere, and when the definition changes, it changes everywhere at once, with an owner and a changelog.

```yaml
# metrics/revenue.yml — defined once, consumed everywhere
metric: revenue
definition:
  measure: order_amount_sum        # SUM(amount) over the orders mart
  filters: [amount >= 0]           # refunds excluded, per contract v3
  time_grain: day
  dimensions: [region, channel, product_category]
owner: finance-analytics
description: 'USD gross merchandise value, refunds excluded, tax included.'
status: certified
```

notes.title: Dimensions, measures, metrics: the vocabulary
notes.body:
- Dimension: an attribute you slice by — region, channel, date. Answers 'by what?'.
- Measure: an aggregation over a fact — SUM(amount), COUNT(orders). Answers 'how much?' — but a raw measure has no business rules yet.
- Metric: a measure + business logic + governance — filters (exclude refunds), grain (daily), definition, owner, certification status. 'Revenue' is a metric; SUM(amount) is a measure.
- Grain discipline: a metric must declare its grain ('one row per day per region'). Comparing a daily metric to a monthly one without alignment is the classic apples-to-oranges error.

```yaml
# measure vs metric: the business logic is what makes it a metric
measures:
  - name: order_amount_sum
    agg: sum
    expr: amount            # raw aggregation, no rules

metrics:
  - name: revenue
    measure: order_amount_sum
    filters: [amount >= 0]  # the business rule lives HERE
    # grain: day  (declared, so consumers can't mis-aggregate)
```

```sql
-- What the layer compiles 'revenue by region, last 30d' into:
SELECT region, DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date) AS day, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM marts.orders
WHERE amount >= 0 AND order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY region, day
```

notes.title: One definition, many consumers
notes.body:
- The same metric definition serves: BI dashboards (the tool queries the layer, not raw tables), notebooks (analysts import certified metrics instead of rewriting logic), and AI assistants (the AI grounds 'revenue' in the defined metric instead of guessing SQL).
- This is the AI-safety payoff from Module 47: an AI that answers 'what was revenue?' through the semantic layer can't invent its own definition — it inherits the certified one.
- Consistency check: pick any metric, query it from two consumers, compare. Divergence means someone bypassed the layer — treat it as an incident, not a curiosity.
- Migration path: don't boil the ocean. Start with your 5 most-disputed metrics, certify them, point the exec dashboard at the layer, expand.

```python
# notebook consumer: certified metric, not rewritten logic
from semantic_layer import metrics
rev = metrics.query('revenue',
                    dimensions=['region'],
                    date_range='last_30d')
# rev is computed from the certified definition — identical to the dashboard's.
```

notes.title: Governance: certification, ownership, deprecation
notes.body:
- Every metric has an owner (team/person) and a status: draft, certified, deprecated. Only certified metrics appear in the exec layer.
- Certification bar: definition reviewed, logic tested (dbt-style tests on the underlying model), semantics documented, stakeholder sign-off.
- Deprecation, not deletion: when 'revenue_v1' is replaced, mark it deprecated with a pointer to v2 and a sunset date — dashboards migrate on a schedule, nothing vanishes overnight.
- Naming discipline: one name, one meaning. 'Revenue' can't also mean 'net revenue' somewhere else — that's net_revenue, a different certified metric.

```yaml
# lifecycle in the metric registry
metric: revenue_v1
status: deprecated
replaced_by: revenue_v2
sunset_date: 2027-01-31
migration_note: 'v2 excludes tax per Finance sign-off 2026-11-15.'
# dashboards on v1 get a migration ticket, not a surprise.
```

cards.back: Business metrics defined once (name, logic, grain, owner) and consumed identically by every dashboard, notebook, and AI query.
The same metric defined differently in each dashboard/notebook — three 'revenues', zero trust. The problem the layer solves.
Dimension: slice-by attribute. Measure: raw aggregation. Metric: measure + business rules + grain + owner + certification.
Comparing a daily metric to a monthly one without alignment is apples-to-oranges; declared grain prevents mis-aggregation.

cards.front: AI-safety payoff of a semantic layer
cards.back: An AI answering through the layer inherits the certified metric definition instead of inventing its own SQL logic.
draft, certified (exec-ready), deprecated (with replacement pointer + sunset date).
Definition reviewed, logic tested, semantics documented, stakeholder sign-off — only certified metrics reach executives.
Deprecate with pointer + sunset date and migration tickets — never silently delete a metric dashboards use.

quiz.q: Three dashboards show three different 'revenue' numbers. The semantic-layer fix is:
choices: Define revenue once (logic, grain, owner, certified) and point all consumers at the definition
quiz.explain: Single definition, many consumers — the sprawl cure. (Module 49)

quiz.q: Which is a METRIC rather than a mere measure?
choices: SUM(amount) with the business rule 'refunds excluded', daily grain, owner, and certified status
quiz.explain: Business rules + grain + governance turn a measure into a metric. (Module 49)

quiz.q: An AI assistant answers 'revenue last quarter' using the semantic layer. The safety benefit:
choices: It inherits the certified definition instead of generating its own possibly-wrong SQL
quiz.explain: Grounding AI in certified definitions prevents invented metric logic. (Module 49)

quiz.q: 'Revenue' is used for both gross and net figures in different reports. Governance fix:
choices: One name, one meaning: keep revenue for the certified gross definition; create net_revenue as a separate certified metric
quiz.explain: Naming discipline: distinct meanings get distinct certified names. (Module 49)

quiz.q: Finance changes the revenue definition (now excludes tax). Rollout discipline:
choices: Version it (revenue_v2), certify, deprecate v1 with sunset date + migration tickets — never silent replacement
quiz.explain: Definition changes are versioned migrations, not silent edits. (Module 49)

quiz.q: A notebook computes revenue with hand-written SQL that differs from the dashboard. You should:
choices: Change the dashboard to match the notebook
Treat the bypass as an incident: point the notebook at the certified metric and reconcile the difference
quiz.explain: Divergence from the layer means someone bypassed it — investigate, don't normalize. (Module 49)

quiz.q: Starting a semantic layer from zero, the pragmatic first step is:
choices: Certify the 5 most-disputed metrics, point the exec dashboard at them, then expand
quiz.explain: Start where the pain is: disputed metrics, visible win, then expand. (Module 49)

quiz.q: A metric's grain is declared as 'day'. An analyst sums its daily values into a monthly total. This is:
choices: Valid only if the metric is additive at that grain — non-additive metrics (ratios, distinct counts) need re-aggregation from base facts
quiz.explain: Grain discipline: additive measures sum safely; ratios and distinct counts don't. (Module 49)

modules.title: XML, XPath, and XSLT for Data Analysts
modules.summary: XML still runs banking feeds, government filings, healthcare HL7, and legacy enterprise integrations — analysts who can't parse it are locked out. This module teaches XML structure, XPath navigation, XSLT transformation, and the Python workflow that turns XML payloads into tidy tables.
objectives: Read XML documents: elements, attributes, namespaces, and well-formedness rules
Write XPath expressions to select nodes, filter by predicates, and extract values
Apply XSLT to transform XML into another XML shape or flat text/CSV
Parse XML in Python (ElementTree/lxml) into pandas-ready records
Handle namespaces and malformed XML without silent data loss

notes.title: XML anatomy: elements, attributes, namespaces
notes.body:
- XML is a tree: elements nest (`<order><id>1</id></order>`), attributes annotate (`<order priority="high">`), one root element per document.
- Well-formed (syntax: tags closed, nested properly) vs valid (conforms to a schema like XSD) — a file can be well-formed but invalid; parsing needs the first, contracts need the second.
- Namespaces (`xmlns:inv="..."`) prevent tag collisions when documents mix vocabularies — `<inv:total>` vs `<tax:total>`. They are the #1 reason XPath queries 'return nothing'.
- Analyst rule: always inspect the raw XML (first 50 lines) before writing any extraction — structure surprises (nested vs flat, attributes vs elements) are the norm.

```xml
<!-- orders.xml: elements carry data, attributes annotate -->
<orders xmlns="urn:il26:orders">
  <order id="1001" priority="high">
    <customer>Acme Corp</customer>
    <total currency="USD">250.00</total>
  </order>
  <order id="1002" priority="normal">
    <customer>Globex</customer>
    <total currency="USD">89.50</total>
  </order>
</orders>
```

notes.title: XPath: SQL for trees
XSLT: transform XML into something usable
notes.body:
- XSLT is a template language that transforms XML -> XML, HTML, or plain text (including CSV). Legacy pipelines use it to reshape feeds before analysts ever see them.
- You won't write stylesheets daily, but you must READ them: when a feed arrives 'wrong', the XSLT in the middle is often the culprit.
- Core: `<xsl:template match="...">` (which nodes), `<xsl:for-each>` (loop), `<xsl:value-of select="..."/>` (extract).
- Modern analyst move: skip XSLT when you can — parse the XML directly in Python (next note). Reach for XSLT when the transform must live in the pipeline, not your script.

```xml
<!-- orders-to-csv.xsl: flatten orders to CSV lines -->
<xsl:stylesheet version="1.0"
  xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
  xmlns:o="urn:il26:orders">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>
  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:text>order_id,customer,total
</xsl:text>
    <xsl:for-each select="//o:order">
      <xsl:value-of select="@id"/><xsl:text>,</xsl:text>
      <xsl:value-of select="o:customer"/><xsl:text>,</xsl:text>
      <xsl:value-of select="o:total"/><xsl:text>
</xsl:text>
    </xsl:for-each>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>
<!-- output: order_id,customer,total / 1001,Acme Corp,250.00 / ... -->
```

notes.title: Python: XML to dataframe without silent loss
notes.body:
- ElementTree (stdlib) handles most feeds; lxml when you need full XPath or broken-HTML tolerance.
- Pattern: iterate record elements, extract fields with namespace-aware finds, build a list of dicts, DataFrame it.
- Namespace handling in ElementTree: use the Clark notation `{urn:il26:orders}order` or register a prefix map — pick one and be consistent.
- Malformed XML: parse defensively — catch ParseError, log the offending file, quarantine it. A parser that silently skips records is worse than one that loudly fails.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
import pandas as pd

NS = {'o': 'urn:il26:orders'}
records = []
try:
    root = ET.parse('orders.xml').getroot()
    for o in root.findall('o:order', NS):
        records.append({
            'order_id': o.get('id'),                       # attribute
            'priority': o.get('priority', 'normal'),       # default if missing
            'customer': o.findtext('o:customer', '', NS),   # element text
            'total': float(o.findtext('o:total', '0', NS)),
            'currency': o.find('o:total', NS).get('currency'),
        })
except ET.ParseError as e:
    raise SystemExit(f'QUARANTINE orders.xml: malformed ({e}) — fix source, do not silently skip')

df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(df, df['total'].sum())
```

cards.back: Well-formed: syntax correct (tags closed/nested). Valid: conforms to a schema (XSD). Parsing needs well-formed; contracts need valid.
All order elements anywhere in the doc with priority attribute = 'high'. // is descendant, [@..] is the predicate filter.
With a default xmlns, //order matches NOTHING — bind a prefix (//o:order) even though the source uses no prefix.
// is SELECT (find nodes), [@x='y'] is WHERE (predicates), /text() is the column (extract content).
A template language transforming XML into other XML, HTML, or text/CSV — read it to debug legacy feed pipelines.
value-of extracts a value (select=...); for-each loops over a node set. template match=... picks which nodes.
Use a prefix map (findall('o:order', NS)) or Clark notation {uri}tag — be consistent, or finds return nothing.
Catch ParseError, log + quarantine the file. Loud failure beats silent record-skipping.

quiz.q: Your XPath //order returns nothing against a document with a default xmlns. The cause and fix:
choices: The namespace trap: bind a prefix to the namespace URI and query //o:order
XPath is case-sensitive about 'order' vs 'Order' only
quiz.explain: Default namespaces require a bound prefix in XPath — the classic gotcha. (Module 50)

quiz.q: Select the customer names of high-priority orders with totals over 100. Best XPath:
quiz.explain: Predicates filter (@attr and child element comparisons), then navigate to the text. (Module 50)

quiz.q: A legacy pipeline delivers a feed in the wrong shape and the XSLT in the middle is suspect. Your first move:
choices: Read the stylesheet: check template match patterns and value-of selects against the actual XML
quiz.explain: XSLT literacy means reading transforms to find the reshape bug. (Module 50)

quiz.q: ElementTree findall('order') returns [] but the file clearly has orders. Likely cause:
choices: Undeclared namespace: use findall('o:order', NS) with the namespace map
quiz.explain: Same namespace trap in Python: unprefixed finds miss namespaced elements. (Module 50)

quiz.q: o.get('priority', 'normal') in the parsing code is an example of:
choices: Defensive extraction: defaulting a missing attribute instead of crashing or inserting None silently
quiz.explain: Explicit defaults document assumptions; silent Nones corrupt downstream logic. (Module 50)

quiz.q: The XML file fails to parse halfway through a 10,000-record feed. Correct handling:
choices: Quarantine the file, log the error, fix the source — never silently process the 5,000 that parsed
quiz.explain: Partial silent processing is the worst outcome; loud quarantine preserves integrity. (Module 50)

quiz.q: When should you reach for XSLT instead of Python parsing?
choices: When the transform must live in the pipeline (reusable, language-neutral) rather than in your one-off script
quiz.explain: XSLT's value is pipeline-resident, reusable transforms; Python wins for analysis-time parsing. (Module 50)

quiz.q: Well-formed but invalid XML means:
choices: Syntax is fine but it violates the agreed schema (XSD) — parsing works, contract validation fails
quiz.explain: Well-formed = parseable; valid = schema-conformant. Both matter, differently. (Module 50)

modules.title: PowerPoint Data Storytelling
modules.summary: Analysis that can't be presented doesn't ship. This module teaches the analyst's presentation craft: narrative structure (situation-complication-resolution), one-message-per-slide, honest chart design, and the delivery habits that turn a findings deck into decisions.
objectives: Structure a findings deck with a narrative arc: situation, complication, resolution, recommendation
Apply one-message-per-slide: headline as the takeaway, visual as the evidence
Design honest charts: proper baselines, labeled axes, no truncated or dual-axis deception
Tailor the deck to the audience: executive summary up front, appendix for the deep dive
Deliver with the decision in mind: recommendation, tradeoffs, ask, and next steps on the final slides

notes.title: Narrative arc: SCR (Situation-Complication-Resolution)
notes.body:
- Situation: shared context everyone agrees on ('Q3 revenue was $4.2M, up 8%').
- Complication: the tension that demands a decision ('...but churn in the West region doubled, erasing the gain').
- Resolution: your recommendation ('Reallocate $200K of acquisition spend to West retention; projected +$600K net').
- The arc turns a data dump into a story with stakes. Executives decide; they don't explore — your deck must arrive at the decision, not invite wandering.
- Test: cover the slide headlines only — they should read as a coherent paragraph. If they don't, the story is broken.

```text
Headline-only test (the deck's story in 5 lines):
1. Q3 revenue grew 8% to $4.2M           (situation)
2. But West-region churn doubled, erasing the gain  (complication)
3. Churn concentrates in customers acquired via discount codes (insight)
4. We recommend shifting $200K to West retention   (resolution)
5. Projected net: +$600K; decision needed by Friday (ask)
```

notes.title: One message per slide: headline = takeaway
notes.body:
- Rule: the slide title states the CONCLUSION ('West churn doubled in Q3'), not the topic ('Churn analysis'). The visual below is the evidence.
- One chart per slide, one takeaway per chart. Two messages = two slides.
- Annotate the chart: circle the spike, label the key value, add the 'so what' in a caption. Never make the audience hunt for the point.
- Data-ink discipline: remove gridlines, 3D effects, and decoration that doesn't encode information. If removing an element changes nothing, remove it.

```text
BEFORE (topic title):  "Churn by region"  + busy 3D bar chart
AFTER (takeaway title): "West churn doubled in Q3, erasing the revenue gain"
                        + flat bars, West bar highlighted, annotation:
                          "2.1% -> 4.3% (n=1,204)"
The audience gets the message in 3 seconds, with or without you talking.
```

notes.title: Honest charts: the integrity checklist
notes.body:
- Baselines: bar charts start at zero — truncated bars exaggerate differences. (Line charts may zoom, but say so.)
- No dual axes with different scales unless you label both loudly — they manufacture correlations.
- Label directly: put values on the bars/points, not just on an axis the audience must interpolate.
- Show uncertainty: error bars or 'n=' counts where the data is thin. A 50% lift on n=12 is noise wearing a costume.
- Sourcing: every chart gets a source + date footnote ('orders mart, 2026-10-06'). Unsourced charts are rumors.
- The Module 47 rule applies: every number traces to a validated query.

```text
Chart integrity checklist (run per visual):
[ ] Bars start at zero (or zoom is disclosed)
[ ] No sneaky dual axes
[ ] Values labeled directly on the visual
[ ] n= shown; uncertainty visible where thin
[ ] Source + as-of date in the footnote
[ ] Number traces to a validated query (Module 47 ladder)
```

notes.title: Audience tailoring and the close
notes.body:
- Executives: BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front. Recommendation on slide 2, supporting evidence after, deep dive in the appendix. Never make them wait 20 slides for the point.
- Peers/technical: methodology earns slides — assumptions, grain, validation. They'll challenge the logic; arm them.
- The close: recommendation (one sentence), tradeoffs (what we give up), the ask (decision/resource/date), next steps with owners.
- Leave-behind: the deck must stand alone — headlines carry the story, appendix holds the proof, notes hold the narration you gave live.

```text
Closing slide template:
  RECOMMENDATION: Shift $200K acquisition -> West retention (Q4).
  TRADEOFF:      East acquisition growth slows ~3%.
  ASK:           Approve by Friday to hit the Q4 window.
  NEXT STEPS:    Ana: retention offer design (10/14) | Ben: spend reallocation (10/15)
  APPENDIX:      methodology, query logic, sensitivity analysis
```

cards.back: Situation (shared context) -> Complication (tension demanding a decision) -> Resolution (recommendation). Turns data dumps into decisions.
Read just the slide headlines: they must form a coherent paragraph. If not, the story is broken.
Title states the CONCLUSION ('West churn doubled'), not the topic ('Churn analysis'); one chart, one takeaway; annotate the point.
Bottom Line Up Front: recommendation on slide 2 for executives; evidence after; deep dive in the appendix.
Bars start at zero — truncated bars exaggerate. Line charts may zoom but must disclose it.
Avoid dual axes with different scales — they manufacture correlations. If used, label both scales loudly.
Every chart: source + as-of date. Unsourced charts are rumors.
Recommendation (one sentence), tradeoffs, the ask (decision/date), next steps with owners, appendix pointer.

quiz.q: Your deck has 20 slides of exploration and the recommendation appears on slide 19. The fix:
choices: BLUF: recommendation on slide 2, evidence after, deep dive in appendix
quiz.explain: Executives decide; don't make them wait 20 slides for the point. (Module 51)

quiz.q: A bar chart shows 4.1% vs 4.3% as dramatically different bar heights. The integrity violation:
choices: Truncated baseline exaggerating a tiny difference — bars must start at zero
quiz.explain: Non-zero baselines manufacture drama; disclose any zoom. (Module 51)

quiz.q: Slide title reads 'Q3 numbers'. Better title:
choices: 'Q3 revenue grew 8%, but West churn erased the gain' — the takeaway, not the topic

quiz.q: A chart shows a 50% lift with n=12 and no uncertainty shown. You should:
choices: Show the n and uncertainty — thin data dressed as a finding is noise in a costume
quiz.explain: Integrity: thin data must show its thinness. (Module 51)

quiz.q: The headline-only test fails — headlines don't form a coherent story. This means:
choices: The narrative arc is broken; restructure around Situation-Complication-Resolution
quiz.explain: Headlines carry the story; incoherence there means incoherence everywhere. (Module 51)

quiz.q: Presenting to engineers who will challenge your methodology, you should:
choices: Give methodology real slides: assumptions, grain, validation — arm them to challenge the logic
quiz.explain: Technical audiences need the logic trail; executives need BLUF. Tailor. (Module 51)

quiz.q: Every number in the deck must:
choices: Trace to a validated query (Module 47 ladder) with source + as-of date footnoted
quiz.explain: Traceability is the integrity backbone of the whole deck. (Module 51)

quiz.q: The deck must stand alone as a leave-behind. This requires:
choices: Headlines carrying the story, appendix with proof, speaker notes with narration — readable without you

multicloudLabs.title: AWS: S3 + Athena Query on the Sample Orders CSV
multicloudLabs.brief: Run one real analytics workload on AWS's free tier: upload the fictional ecom_orders CSV to S3, query it with Athena's serverless SQL engine (pay-per-query, no servers), then tear everything down. You will touch a bucket, a table definition, and a query — and leave no billable residue.
steps: Sign in to the AWS console and choose a region close to you (e.g. us-east-1); do ALL work in this one region so resources are easy to find at cleanup
Create an S3 bucket with a globally unique name (e.g. il26-lab-<yourname>-<date>); keep Block Public Access ON and versioning OFF
Upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv to the bucket under s3://<bucket>/raw/ecom_orders.csv
Open Athena, run the one-time setup: set the query-result location to s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ (Athena needs a place to write results)

In the Athena query editor, create the table: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE orders (order_id string, order_date string, customer_id string, region string, channel string, product_category string, amount double, discount_code string) ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' STORED AS TEXTFILE LOCATION 's3://<bucket>/raw/' TBLPROPERTIES ('skip.header.line.count'='1')
Run the workload query: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC — confirm it matches your local DuckDB totals
Check the Athena query history panel: note the 'Data scanned' amount for your queries (this is what Athena bills on — small CSV means fractions of a cent)
multicloudLabs.workload: Athena serverless SQL over the S3-hosted ecom_orders CSV: revenue and order counts by region, reconciled against the local DuckDB totals from TL-02. The workload demonstrates decoupled storage (S3) and serverless compute (Athena) — the core cloud analytics pattern.
costGuardrails: Athena's free tier covers a small monthly query-data allowance; a 15-row CSV scans kilobytes — stay on tiny files and this lab costs essentially nothing
S3 free tier covers a small amount of storage and requests monthly; one CSV plus query results is far below it — do not upload large datasets
Keep everything in ONE region; cross-region data movement is where surprise charges come from
Do not enable S3 versioning, replication, or intelligent-tiering on the lab bucket — all add cost for zero lab benefit
Set a billing alert (e.g. $1) in the Billing console before starting — the habit matters more than the threshold
cleanup: Athena: no persistent compute to delete (serverless), but note your query history for the report
S3: delete s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ contents, then s3://<bucket>/raw/ecom_orders.csv, then delete the bucket itself
Verify: S3 console shows zero buckets matching il26-lab-*; Billing dashboard shows no active resources
Record the final 'Data scanned' totals and confirm the month-to-date bill is $0.00 before closing the lab
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Athena query results match local DuckDB region totals exactly; lab bucket deleted; billing dashboard shows $0.00; 'Data scanned' recorded.

multicloudLabs.title: Azure: Storage + Synapse Serverless SQL on the Sample Orders CSV
multicloudLabs.brief: Run the same workload on Azure: land the fictional ecom_orders CSV in Azure Storage and query it with Synapse's serverless SQL pool (pay per terabyte scanned, no cluster to manage). Free-account framing throughout, full teardown at the end.
steps: Sign in to the Azure portal; confirm you are on a free account/trial subscription and note its expiry date before creating anything
Create a resource group named il26-lab-rg in a region near you — everything goes here so cleanup is one deletion
Create a Storage account (standard performance, LRS redundancy — the cheapest options) inside il26-lab-rg
In the storage account, create a container named raw and upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv

Open Synapse Studio, create a serverless SQL pool workspace (or use an existing one), and run: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(CAST(amount AS FLOAT)),2) AS revenue FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/raw/ecom_orders.csv', FORMAT='CSV', PARSER_VERSION='2.0', HEADER_ROW=TRUE) AS o GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC
Reconcile the results against your local DuckDB totals — same numbers, different cloud
Check the Synapse monitoring view: note the data processed by the query (this is the billing meter)
multicloudLabs.workload: Synapse serverless SQL over the Storage-hosted ecom_orders CSV via OPENROWSET: revenue and order counts by region, reconciled against local DuckDB totals. Demonstrates Azure's decoupled storage-plus-serverless-query pattern, the direct analog of the AWS lab.
costGuardrails: Serverless SQL pools bill per terabyte of data processed; a 15-row CSV processes megabytes — keep files tiny and queries few
Free accounts include limited monthly credits: this lab uses a negligible fraction, but never run ad-hoc exploratory queries against large files on a free account
Use the cheapest storage options (standard, LRS) — premium tiers and geo-redundancy multiply cost for no lab benefit
Do NOT provision a dedicated SQL pool or Spark pool — those bill per hour while running and are unnecessary for this workload
Put everything in the single il26-lab-rg resource group so nothing billable hides outside it
cleanup: Delete the entire resource group il26-lab-rg (this removes the storage account, container, and any Synapse artifacts in one action)
Verify: portal search for il26-lab-rg returns nothing; storage accounts list shows no lab account
Check Cost Management: confirm the subscription shows no ongoing charges from the lab resources
Record the data-processed totals from Synapse monitoring for your lab report
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Query results match local DuckDB totals; resource group il26-lab-rg deleted and verified gone; Cost Management shows no ongoing lab charges.

multicloudLabs.title: GCP: BigQuery Sandbox Query on the Sample Orders Dataset
multicloudLabs.brief: Run the workload on Google Cloud's BigQuery sandbox — which lets you query without even adding a billing account. Load the fictional ecom_orders CSV, run the regional revenue analysis, and clean up the dataset. The sandbox's limits ARE the guardrails here.
steps: Sign in to the Google Cloud console and create/select a project named il26-lab; open BigQuery Studio
Confirm you are in sandbox mode (no billing account attached — the console labels it); note the sandbox's table expiration behavior before loading data
Create a dataset named lab_orders in a US region; upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv as a table named orders (auto-detect schema, header row = 1)
Run the workload query: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS revenue FROM `il26-lab.lab_orders.orders` GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC
Reconcile against local DuckDB totals; then run one variant: monthly revenue trend with DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)
Open the query job details: note bytes processed and slot time — this is what BigQuery meters
multicloudLabs.workload: BigQuery SQL over the uploaded ecom_orders table: regional revenue/orders plus a monthly trend, reconciled against local DuckDB totals. Demonstrates the warehouse-native pattern (data loaded INTO the engine) as contrast to the S3/Storage query-in-place pattern of the other two labs.
costGuardrails: The BigQuery sandbox requires no billing account and grants a monthly free query allowance — but sandbox tables EXPIRE (default 60 days) and some features are restricted; know these limits before relying on sandbox data

With billing enabled later, BigQuery's free tier covers a monthly query-data allowance — the 15-row table processes kilobytes; never point ad-hoc queries at multi-terabyte public datasets on a free tier without checking bytes-processed first
Always check the query validator's 'bytes processed' estimate BEFORE running — it is displayed in the editor and is your pre-flight cost check
Keep the lab to the two queries specified; exploratory querying against large tables is the classic free-tier-burn mistake
cleanup: Delete the lab_orders dataset (deleting the dataset removes the orders table with it)
Verify: BigQuery explorer shows no lab_orders dataset under il26-lab
Optionally delete the il26-lab project itself for a fully clean slate
Record bytes-processed totals from both query jobs for your lab report
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Both queries' results match local DuckDB totals; lab_orders dataset deleted and verified gone; bytes-processed recorded for both jobs.
